profiles.meeting_scenario: An Islamic bank's digital finance unit is troubleshooting why a pilot blockchain-based smart contract for a murabaha financing product was flagged by both the Shariah review desk and operations team after a live dry-run. In the dry-run, a customer's late-payment case could not be rescheduled without redeploying logic, and the audit log showed a proxy upgrade path that operations believed was acceptable while Shariah reviewers called it too open-ended. The meeting is between the product implementation lead and the Shariah governance specialist to diagnose the real source of the problem, determine whether the issue is with immutability, contract design, or governance controls, and agree on a corrective approach for the next pilot iteration. The agenda is to review what failed in the dry-run, identify the root cause, and decide what a 'fix' should include before the pilot is shown again to the internal review committee. The expected outcome is an agreed troubleshooting direction: keep the smart-contract approach, but revise the architecture and controls around rescheduling and upgradeability.

members.name: Amina Rahman
members.expertise: Enterprise blockchain deployment, smart-contract architecture, banking systems integration
members.background: Amina previously led digitization projects at a conventional bank before moving into Islamic banking innovation, where she now oversees technical pilots connecting financing workflows to permissioned blockchain infrastructure.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve momentum on the pilot and avoid the conclusion that blockchain is unsuitable for Islamic financing products; she is also concerned that adding too many approvals or narrow conditions will make the architecture impractical to maintain.
hidden_assumptions: If the economic terms visible to the customer remain governed by approved product rules, changing executable logic through a controlled proxy is not a substantive contract rewrite.
A workable 'rescheduling' mechanism can be implemented as parameter updates to payment timing while keeping the underlying financing contract intact.
When reviewers ask for 'flexibility,' they mainly want exceptional operational handling already authorized by policy, not case-by-case new legal drafting on-chain.
An adequate fix is one that prevents operational dead-ends in real customer hardship cases without requiring redeployment of every contract instance.

members.name: Dr. Farid Yusuf
members.expertise: Islamic contract structuring, Shariah review processes, product-governance controls
members.background: Dr. Farid trained in fiqh al-muamalat and later joined banking governance teams, where he reviews whether digital implementations preserve the intent and procedural safeguards of approved Islamic finance products.
members.private_state: He wants to ensure the pilot does not create the impression that smart contracts can autonomously alter Shariah-sensitive obligations; he is particularly worried about governance ambiguity more than technical elegance.
hidden_assumptions: If a customer's obligations are 'restructured' or 'rescheduled,' that action is only valid when the relevant discretionary review and approval path is preserved as part of the implementation, not merely referenced in policy documents.
An 'upgradeable' contract is acceptable only if its practical scope is tightly bounded to pre-approved contingencies rather than open technical discretion after deployment.
When the team says the contract is 'immutable,' he assumes this should mean the governing obligation cannot be changed by technical administrators except through specifically sanctioned pathways.
A true fix must close governance ambiguity for Shariah review, even if the system is already operationally workable.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the next version needs 'flexibility' for hardship cases.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Amina means prebuilt technical adaptability in code, such as adjustable schedule parameters and modular logic reachable through a proxy without redeploying each financing instance.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Dr. Farid means preservation of Shariah-governed discretionary treatment, where flexibility is the institution's ability to consider a case and apply approved relief within clearly delimited conditions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In this domain, 'flexibility' sounds obviously desirable to both sides, and each hears the other's statements as supportive of their own interpretation because both technical adaptability and discretionary accommodation are positively associated with iḥsān.

misalignment_points.topic: What exactly was the problem in the dry-run
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the dry-run failure' and 'the exception case' as if discussing the same event.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Amina is primarily thinking of the Tuesday sandbox incident where the due-date field could not be updated for a simulated hardship customer without redeploying the financing logic.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Dr. Farid is primarily thinking of the committee review note attached to that dry-run, which criticized the broad admin upgrade path in the proxy controller rather than the due-date update itself.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both incidents occurred in the same pilot review cycle and are bundled in project memory as one 'failure,' so each participant can respond coherently without noticing they are diagnosing different objects.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a 'fix' before the next review
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want a 'fix' that can go back to committee next week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Amina believes the issue is fixed if the product can execute a rescheduling scenario without manual workaround and with an auditable on-chain record.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Dr. Farid believes the issue is fixed only if the implementation demonstrates that any post-deployment change is limited to pre-approved scenarios and cannot be interpreted as unrestricted alteration of contractual obligations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both standards sound like normal completion criteria for a troubleshooting meeting, and neither is so obviously incompatible that it would prompt direct clarification during a cooperative discussion.

misalignment_points.topic: What the agreed upgrade path includes
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to use an 'upgradeable proxy' with controls.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Amina assumes the proxy can cover future operational patches related to payment schedule handling, notification timing, and edge-case logic, so long as admin rights are controlled and logged.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Dr. Farid assumes the proxy is only for narrowly specified, pre-approved contingencies such as hardship rescheduling mechanics already described in the product papers, not for broader behavior changes after deployment.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'with controls' gives a strong sense of alignment while hiding a difference in boundary assumptions; each thinks the other naturally understands the acceptable scope of those controls.

turns.inner_thought: We need to keep this grounded in the pilot staying viable. The dry-run failure, to me, was straightforward: in Tuesday's sandbox case, we hit an operational dead-end because the due-date handling was too rigid and we couldn't adjust the schedule for a hardship customer without redeploying logic. If we overreact and conclude blockchain is the problem, this pilot will stall. What we actually need is more flexibility in the contract design so approved product behavior can still be executed cleanly.
turns.utterance: Thanks, Farid. From my side, the main takeaway from the dry-run failure was that the current build just didn't have enough flexibility to deal with the exception case cleanly. The product flow held up until that point, but once we needed to handle that scenario, the architecture became too rigid.

turns.inner_thought: I agree flexibility is necessary, but the real concern from my side was the review note, not only the operational snag. The dry-run failure showed governance ambiguity because the proxy controller looked too open-ended. If this implementation gives the impression that administrators can alter Shariah-sensitive obligations after deployment without tightly bounded pathways, committee will not be comfortable. I need to steer this toward controlled governance, not just technical convenience.
turns.utterance: I agree that we need flexibility, but what concerned me in the dry-run failure was that the current setup appeared to allow changes without sufficiently bounded governance. So for me the issue was not only that the exception case was awkward to process, but also that the controls around it were not yet clear enough.

turns.inner_thought: He's acknowledging flexibility, good. Then the practical answer is obvious: in a hardship scenario, we should be able to reschedule by updating timing parameters without redeploying every murabaha instance. That's exactly why we introduced the upgradeable proxy in the first place. If the proxy is controlled and logged, I don't see that as a substantive rewrite. We cannot make operations redeploy contracts every time a customer needs accommodated timing.
turns.utterance: Right, and in that sort of hardship situation we should be able to reschedule without redeploying the financing contract each time. My assumption was that the upgradeable proxy already in the architecture would let us support that in a controlled way.

turns.inner_thought: Rescheduling itself is not the problem. The problem is whether the implementation preserves the same approval path and conditions that the product papers require. If the system can only do this because there is broad technical discretion after deployment, that is not acceptable. An upgradeable proxy can be acceptable, but only if it is constrained to contingencies already sanctioned, not treated as a general-purpose mechanism.
turns.utterance: Rescheduling is acceptable in principle, yes, but only where the implementation reflects the same approved conditions and approvals that the product papers already assume. If we are relying on the upgradeable proxy with controls, then those controls need to mirror that framework rather than sit beside it.

turns.inner_thought: I think we're still aligned. To me this is mainly an immutability design issue: the contract was too frozen at the wrong layer. We can parameterize payment dates and hardship states so the same exception case is handled natively, with an audit trail, and that should count as a fix for next week. That avoids manual workarounds and avoids redeploying all instances.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I would treat the root cause primarily as an immutability design problem. If we parameterize the relevant payment dates and hardship states, the next version should be able to handle the same exception case natively, which would give us a fix we can take back to committee next week.

turns.inner_thought: I don't think the root cause is immutability by itself. The issue is ambiguity about what post-deployment discretion exists. Committee will focus on whether administrators can alter obligations through a broad pathway. A true fix before next week must make the boundary explicit and reviewable. If that remains vague, a working technical demo still will not solve the governance problem.
turns.utterance: I would frame the root cause a little differently. For me, the main concern is ambiguity around what administrators are permitted to alter after deployment. So the fix needs to make that boundary explicit before the next committee review, otherwise we may still have the same question even if the process works better operationally.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, we can package it that way. I don't want this turning into a debate that blocks the pilot. We can keep the upgradeable proxy, tighten admin permissions, improve audit logs, and show restricted access. That should satisfy governance while preserving enough room for operations to respond to real hardship cases and edge cases without rebuilding the architecture every time.
turns.utterance: That's fine with me. We can keep the upgradeable proxy with controls, make the audit trail more visible, and tighten restricted admin access so operations can still respond when a real hardship case comes through.

turns.inner_thought: Good, but I need to anchor what 'with controls' means. I can agree if upgrades are tied only to pre-approved contingencies already contemplated in the product governance materials. What I do not want is any room for the system to be perceived as enabling open-ended contractual modification after deployment. If I state that plainly enough, perhaps the design note will reflect it.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I would add that those controls should tie any upgrade path to pre-approved contingencies and should not leave room for open-ended contractual modification. If that is clear, the governance position becomes much easier to defend.

turns.inner_thought: That still sounds consistent to me. I can revise the code so the contract is more flexible while keeping the record immutable where it matters. The key outcome is that future dry-runs do not end with manual intervention because the schedule handling is trapped in rigid logic. If we log every change and preserve the financing record, that should be enough.
turns.utterance: Understood. I can revise the code so the contract is more flexible while still preserving immutability at the record level, and that should also help us avoid manual intervention in future dry-runs.

turns.inner_thought: I need the documentation to make explicit that the exception case sits within the approved restructuring and rescheduling framework, not as a free-standing technical capability. If that is shown properly, committee can assess the implementation against the product approvals rather than against a vague idea of technical flexibility.
turns.utterance: That would help. When you revise the design note, please show how the exception case is handled under the approved restructuring and rescheduling framework. That linkage will matter a lot in the next review.

turns.inner_thought: I'll package this as a practical fix: parameterized hardship handling plus the same proxy pattern, but with stronger governance documentation. That should get us through committee without having to abandon maintainability. I still need enough scope in the architecture to cover schedule handling, notifications, and other edge conditions later, but I don't need to argue that now.
turns.utterance: All right. I'll prepare a fix for next week that combines parameterized hardship handling with the existing proxy pattern, tightened up with clearer governance documentation and controls.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds workable if the materials really demonstrate both dimensions I care about: practical flexibility for hardship treatment and clear limits on what may change after deployment. I assume she means the flexibility already contemplated by approved governance pathways. If the draft reflects that, I can support it going back to committee.
turns.utterance: Good. Send me the updated materials once they're ready, and I'll review them with that in mind. If the fix shows both practical flexibility and clear limits on what can change after deployment, we should be in a better position for committee next week.
